strengths: Segmenting 3D structures into distinct local components is an insightful approach.
The reconstruction method for these local structures is intriguing and presents a unique strategy.
There is a marked novelty in the concept of pre-training 3D molecules through local structures, despite the base model being a straightforward extension of TokenGT enhanced with 3D coordinates.
The empirical performance is OK for some of the fine tuning tasks, although still not consistently solid.
The main method in the paper is interesting conceptually and somewhat original as it combines a graph token representation with a decomposition of a small molecule into smaller 3D structural units.
The downstream application on MoleculeNet is significant, and the application on the open graph benchmark is useful for context, although the particular table 2 is misleading.
The introduction is reasonably clear, however, other parts of the paper have problems with the language or formalism.
The paper is well-motivated through the concept of molecular local structure and the introduced approach yields good novelty.
The presentation is mostly clear and the method is easy to follow.
weaknesses: The base model's simple strategy of appending 3D features to token embeddings may compromise the essential equivariance of 3D molecules; specifically, the direct concatenation of 3D coordinates to node embeddings, without considering rotational or translational invariance, could lead to a model that is sensitive to arbitrary orientations of the input molecule.

The description of the training objective section lacks clarity; it is unclear how the local structure reconstruction is implemented, how separate mask indicators for center atoms, edges, and leaf atoms are used to generate reconstruction targets, how the loss function is computed across these different reconstruction tasks, and whether they are weighted differently.
The paper does not disclose reconstruction accuracy on the pretraining dataset, making it difficult to assess whether the model is effectively capturing the 3D structural information.

The experimental comparisons should include additional 3D molecular datasets such as QM9 and GEOM-drug; the current evaluation is limited to the OGBLSC-PCQM4Mv2 dataset and significantly lags behind SOTA methods, with insufficient explanation for the underperformance.
The layout of the paper requires revision; the Algorithm should be positioned before page 10 or in an appendix rather than after the references.

The geometrical justification of tetrahedra as the simplest polyhedron might make sense, but in chemistry it makes much less sense; the authors show benzene in Figure 1b, which has a 120-degree bonding pattern (planar‑trigonal) that is not a tetrahedron and has very different local symmetries.
The ablation studies are unconvincing; the authors do not evaluate the role of the actual innovations introduced (tetrahedra vs. point‑wise generation) or the role of edge information.
It is unclear how the method handles atoms with more than four bonds (e.g., sulfur, phosphorus).
The statement “We attribute this to the different 3D structures molecules exhibit in liposome compounds.” is ambiguous; it is not explained what different structures are being referred to.
All the biochemistry prediction tasks are actually properties of the graph, not the 3D structure, raising the question of what 3D structure is being used.
The paper can use a lot of rewriting in the methods and experimental results sections.
Table 1 does not correctly highlight the best and second‑best results (e.g., the BACE column where two 2D models outperform LEGO).
Table 2 is missing the vast majority of best‑performing models from the Open Graph Benchmark large‑scale challenge.

The comparison in Table 2 omits the top two entries that are models included in Table 1; consequently, the LEGO model would rank 9th in the validation metric with a substantial gap compared to Unimol published at last year’s ICLR.
It would be useful if the authors submitted their model to the benchmark to see the performance on the test set.

The text contains many rushed or unclear sentences (e.g., the first sentence on page 8, undefined d_p on page 5, “way to increase the and generalizability” on page 6, and several other unclear fragments on pages 7).
The ablation study is not helpful; the perturbation of the model is too limited, and Table 3 suggests that the parameters are not optimal.
The random‑perturbation pretraining described in Table 4 is not explained clearly enough.

The experimental results seem insufficient to support the empirical superiority of the proposed approach; the method could be further improved through a more careful design of the backbone or enhancements of the training objective.

The authors should consider evaluating on other benchmarks or setups (e.g., QM9, MD17) where better utilization of 3D structural information could bring more benefits, as the current experimental evaluations may not meet the ICLR bar.
